content: The data available was not of sufficient quality to establish a definitive association between Stachybotrys chartarum and acute idiopathic pulmonary hemorrhage (AIPH). Additionally, evidence from other sources supporting a causal role of S. chartarum in AIPH is limited. 1. AIPH does not align with historical accounts of illnesses in humans or animals caused by S. chartarum or other toxigenic fungi. 2. Clusters of AIPH have not been reported in other flood-prone areas where the growth of S. chartarum or similar fungi might be expected. 3. The mold-disease association observed in the Cleveland investigation was not replicated in a similar cluster investigation in Chicago (CDC, unpublished data, May 1997). chartarum are not adequately substantiated by the scientific evidence produced in the CDC investigation. Protease inhibitors (PIs) and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), used in the treatment of HIV, are substrates that can inhibit or induce cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzymes. Rifamycins, used in tuberculosis (TB) treatment, induce CYP450 and can significantly reduce blood levels of antiretroviral drugs. These interactions, termed drug-drug interactions, are bidirectional, as antiretroviral agents can also affect rifamycin blood levels. Updated guidelines from CDC scientists and external consultants provide recommendations for managing these interactions. Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), another class of antiretroviral agents, are not metabolized by CYP450, and their concurrent use with rifamycins does not require dose adjustments. Rifabutin, rather than rifampin, was previously recommended for TB treatment in patients taking PIs or NNRTIs. However, new data suggest that rifampin can be used in specific scenarios: 1. In patients whose antiretroviral regimen includes the NNRTI efavirenz and two NRTIs. 2. In patients whose regimen includes the PI ritonavir and one or more NRTIs. 3. In patients on a combination of two PIs (ritonavir and either saquinavir hard-gel or soft-gel capsules). The updated guidelines also recommend reducing the rifabutin dose (150 mg two or three times per week) when co-administered with ritonavir and increasing the rifabutin dose (450–600 mg daily or two to three times per week) when used with efavirenz. Ritonavir has the highest potency in inhibiting CYP450, which increases plasma concentrations of co-administered PIs, a property exploited in combination therapies (e.g., low-dose ritonavir with saquinavir to increase saquinavir levels). For patients treated with two PIs, drug interaction complexity increases. Co-administration of saquinavir soft-gel capsules (SGC) with usual-dose rifabutin (300 mg daily or two to three times per week) is possible, but pharmacokinetic data and clinical experience are limited. Saquinavir (SGC or hard-gel capsules) with ritonavir can be co-administered with usual-dose rifampin (600 mg daily or two to three times per week) or reduced-dose rifabutin (150 mg two or three times per week), though data are limited. Saquinavir with rifampin (without ritonavir) is not recommended due to significant reductions in saquinavir concentrations. If ritonavir and rifabutin are used together, a substantially reduced rifabutin dose (150 mg two or three times per week) is recommended. Co-administration of ritonavir with usual-dose rifampin (600 mg daily or two to three times per week) is possible, though data are limited. Limited but favorable clinical experience exists with indinavir co-administered with reduced-dose rifabutin (150 mg daily) or usual-dose rifabutin (300 mg two or three times per week). Indinavir with rifampin is not recommended due to marked reductions in indinavir concentrations. Limited clinical experience exists with nelfinavir co-administered with reduced-dose rifabutin (150 mg daily) or usual-dose rifabutin (300 mg two or three times per week). Nelfinavir with rifampin is not recommended due to significant reductions in nelfinavir concentrations. Amprenavir with reduced-dose rifabutin (150 mg daily) or usual-dose rifabutin (300 mg two or three times per week) is a possibility, but no published clinical experience exists. Amprenavir with rifampin is not recommended due to marked reductions in amprenavir concentrations. Nevirapine with usual-dose rifabutin (300 mg daily or two to three times per week) is a possibility based on pharmacokinetic data, but no published clinical experience exists. Data are insufficient to determine whether dose adjustments are necessary when rifampin is co-administered with nevirapine. Therefore, rifampin and nevirapine should only be used together if clearly indicated and with careful monitoring. Delavirdine is contraindicated with either rifabutin or rifampin due to significant reductions in delavirdine concentrations. Efavirenz with increased-dose rifabutin (450–600 mg daily or two to three times per week) is a possibility, though data are limited.
